chunks: Among what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Zurārah, who said:
I said to Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام: I am a merchant man; I go about and engage in trade. So how can I manage the noon decline time and maintain the prayer of zawāl, and how many rakʿahs is it prayed?

He said: You pray eight rakʿahs when the sun declines, and two rakʿahs after al-ẓuhr, and two rakʿahs before al-ʿaṣr; these are twelve rakʿahs. And you pray two rakʿahs after al-maghrib, and after the middle of the night thirteen rakʿahs, among them al-witr and among them the two rakʿahs of al-fajr. Those are twenty-seven rakʿahs besides the obligatory prayer. All of this is supererogatory and not obligatory. Indeed, the one who abandons the obligatory prayer is a kāfir, but the one who abandons this is not a kāfir; rather, it is a sin, because it is recommended that when a man performs an act of good, he should be constant in it.

So this hadith contains Zurārah's mention of his excuse due to trade and other matters. Thus, the Imam عليه السلام allowed him to suffice with less than fifty, which indicates what we have mentioned: that the prescribed sunnah is fifty-one rakʿahs so long as there is no excuse there.

key_terms.التِّجَارَةِ: trade or commercial occupation serving here as an excuse
key_terms.الْفَرِيضَةِ: the obligatory prayer required by religious law
key_terms.الْمَسْنُونَ: that which is established as sunnah or recommended practice
key_terms.الْوَتْرُ: the witr prayer included within the night prayer
key_terms.تَطَوُّعٌ: supererogatory worship that is recommended rather than obligatory
key_terms.صَلَاةِ الزَّوَالِ: the recommended prayer performed at the time of the sun’s decline
key_terms.مَعْصِيَةٌ: an act of disobedience or sin

ai.seo_question: How many recommended daily rakʿahs should be prayed when a person has an excuse such as trade, and are they obligatory?
ai.summary: This hadith explains a reduced schedule of recommended daily prayers for one who has an excuse such as being occupied with trade. It distinguishes clearly between obligatory prayers and supererogatory prayers, stating that abandonment of the obligatory prayer is not like abandonment of the recommended prayers, while still emphasizing the virtue of consistency in good deeds.
